blogs.title: The Subjective Intent Fallacy: How *Santos v. Kimmel* Reaffirms the Objective Standard in Transformative Fair Use
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Second Circuit's rigorous application of the 'transformative' prong of the fair use doctrine in *Santos*. It focuses specifically on the court's rejection of Santos's argument regarding Kimmel's bad faith and subjective intent. By citing *Andy Warhol Foundation*, the decision underscores that fair use analysis relies on what a 'reasonable observer' perceives, rather than the subjective motivations of either the creator or the parodist. This article explores why this objective standard is crucial for protecting satire and commentary, preventing litigants from weaponizing copyright based on their personal feelings about a parody.

blogs.title: Behind the Cameo Curtain: Third-Party Beneficiaries and Contract Formation in Digital Platforms
blogs.description: Moving beyond constitutional copyright questions, this blog examines the Second Circuit's handling of Santos's state law contract claims. The opinion provides a sharp reminder of the strict requirements for establishing third-party beneficiary status under Illinois law and meeting-of-minds standards under New York law. Specifically, it dissects why a public figure cannot automatically enforce Terms of Service agreements between a platform (Cameo) and its users (Kimmel). This analysis offers practical guidance for lawyers navigating disputes involving digital platforms where one party attempts to sue over breaches of contracts to which they are not signatories.

, {\"title\": \"From Parody to Pleadin.description: While much attention will be paid to the First Amendment implications of this ruling, this post zooms in on the procedural victory regarding Santos's fraudulent inducement claim. The court affirmed dismissal because Santos failed to plead 'out-of-pocket losses,' a fundamental element under New York common law fraud statutes. This discussion highlights how substantive tort requirements can serve as an efficient gatekeeper at the motion-to-dismiss stage, effectively barring recovery even when deceptive conduct (using fake names) is admitted or alleged.
